item.research_question: Which deconvolution-based peak profile analysis methods (conventional vs. modified) best characterize the dislocation structure and crystallite size of CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy during plastic deformation, and how do these structural parameters evolve with strain?
item.processing_route: Arc melting of pure elements (12 remelts, flipped every 2nd melt) to form ~30g ingots; wire discharge machining into cylinders (5 mm diameter, 8 mm height); axial compression at room temperature with a strain rate of ~8.4·10−3 s−1 to engineering strains of 0.00, 25.00, 37.50, 42.50, 47.50, and 55.00%
item.test_conditions: Synchrotron X-ray diffraction (transmission mode, beamline 5-A, VEPP-4) using 50.12 keV photons (0.0247 nm wavelength); microhardness tests (HV0.1) on deformed specimens
key_findings: The conventional Williamson-Hall (cWH) method shows poor correlation with experimental data, with adjusted R² values ranging from 0.1 to 0.5.
Correcting for elastic modulus (WHEhkl method) significantly reduces approximation error compared to cWH.
The modified Williamson-Hall (mWH) method provides the best fit, yielding R² values above 0.8.
Dislocation density increases with strain and reaches a plateau at an engineering strain of 47.5%.
The average dislocation density at the plateau is approximately 40·10¹⁴ m⁻².
Crystallite size (CSR) decreases with strain up to 41.5–47.5% and remains constant thereafter.
Microhardness increases significantly up to 42.5% strain but shows little change at higher strains.
The Wilkens parameter (M) increases continuously, indicating a disordered dislocation structure rather than a cell structure.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the failure of conventional methods to the elastic anisotropy and intrinsically high lattice distortion of the HEA. They argue that the modified methods (mWH/mWA) succeed by incorporating a dislocation model of strain anisotropy and contrast factors. The saturation of dislocation density at 47.5% strain is explained by the classical concept where nucleation and annihilation rates of dislocations become equal. The continuous increase in the Wilkens parameter suggests the dislocation structure becomes more disordered without forming a self-screening cell structure due to insufficient strain.
item.limitations: The authors state that the strain applied was not sufficient for the formation of a cell-like structure, which typically leads to a decrease in the dislocation outer cut-off radius and Wilkens parameter.
item.future_work: The authors recommend the mWH method for other researchers studying the structure of deformed HEAs and suggest that the approach can be applied to analyze defects in polycrystalline materials with various crystal structures.
quotes: Peak profile analysis shows that the dislocation density of the CoCrFeMnNi alloy subjected to axial compression increases with increase in strain and reaches plateau at a strain of 47.5%.
